Paper Title: Contributions to the Study of SMS Spam Filtering: New Collection and Results
Authors: Tiago A. Almeida; José María Gómez Hidalgo; Akebo Yamakami
Journal/Conference: Proc. 11th ACM Symposium on Document Engineering (DocEng '11), Mountain View, CA, USA, 19-22 Sep 2011, pp. 259-262
Research Objective: Release a public, real, non-encoded SMS spam corpus and report baseline results of established classifiers on it. Motivation: few public SMS corpora, few features per message, and idiom/abbreviation-heavy text.
Dataset Used: SMS Spam Collection v.1, assembled from Grumbletext (425 spam), NUS SMS Corpus (3,375 ham), C. Tagg thesis (450 ham) and SMS Spam Corpus v.0.1 Big (1,002 ham, 322 spam).
Dataset Size: 5,574 messages: 4,827 ham (86.60%) and 747 spam (13.40%); 81,175 tokens in total.
Methodology and Models: 14 classifier entries (several naive Bayes variants, boosted NB, linear SVM, MDL, kNN with K=1/3/5, C4.5, boosted C4.5, PART) with two tokenizers (tok1, tok2); WEKA defaults; no stop-word removal, stemming or dimensionality reduction. EM clustering and a trivial rejector are used as baselines. Near-duplicate check uses N-gram string matching.
Key Findings: [Reported] Linear SVM + tok1 was best by MCC: spam caught 83.10%, blocked ham 0.18%, accuracy 97.64%, MCC 0.893. Boosted NB, boosted C4.5 and PART reached 97.50% accuracy (MCC 0.887); the authors state the best four were not statistically different. Trivial rejector accuracy 86.95%. Authors conclude SVM is a good baseline.
Evaluation Metrics: Spam caught (SC%), blocked ham (BH%), accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC).
Advantages: Public and real messages; transparent protocol; duplicate analysis reported; ham-blocking rate reported separately from accuracy.
Limitations: [Authors] Limited public data, few features per message, idioms and abbreviations. [Our reading] One fixed split (first 30% train, remaining 70% test), no cross-validation or variance; spam and ham come largely from different sources, so source may correlate with label; English only; the task is unsolicited-spam filtering, not phishing; the text read does not describe TF-IDF weighting.
Relevance to Our Project: FOUNDATIONAL baseline. Supports a linear SVM as a strong, simple short-text baseline and the habit of reporting ham-blocking rate. It does not validate TF-IDF specifically and says nothing about phishing, Malayalam or Manglish.
Research Gap or Opportunity: No Malayalam, Manglish or code-mixed counterpart; no phishing labels; single-split evaluation.

Paper Title: Transformer Attention-Driven Concept Extraction for Efficient Smishing Detection
Authors: Zahriya Lawal Hassan; Nor Fazlida Mohd Sani; Muhammad Daniel Hafiz Abdullah; Norwati Mustapha
Journal/Conference: Artificial Intelligence and Applications (Bon View), 2026, Vol. 00(00), pp. 1-9; online 10 Mar 2026
Research Objective: Improve accuracy and interpretability of smishing detection by grouping regex-derived message signatures into textual, structural and behavioural concepts, encoded with BERT and analysed through attention weights.
Dataset Used: UCI SMS Spam Collection (Almeida et al.). The authors renamed the spam label 'smish' because they consider the two labels similar.
Dataset Size: About 5,572 messages (4,825 ham; 747 labelled smish); stratified 80:20 split.
Languages and Scripts: English (Latin script). Multilingual work is listed as future work.
Methodology and Models: Regex signatures; three concept categories; BERT [CLS] embedding per concept; fully connected classifier; LR, RF and SVM baselines on the same BERT embeddings; ablation by concept.
Key Findings: [Reported] BERT + FC: accuracy 99.32%, precision 98.01%, recall 99.42%, F1 98.71%, ROC-AUC 99.95%. BERT + RF 98.90% accuracy, + SVM 98.70%, + LR 98.55%. Ablation: behavioural concept alone gave 99.62% accuracy and F1 97.47%.
Advantages: Interpretable concept categories; baselines on identical features; discusses the efficiency trade-off (MobileBERT).
Limitations: [Authors] BERT is costly for mobile deployment; multilingual use is future work. [Our reading] Results measure UCI spam detection relabelled as smishing; single stratified split; the fusion step (final vector concatenates smishing and ham representations) needs checking for label leakage; the behavioural-only accuracy (99.62%) exceeds the full model (99.32%) without explanation; the SVM baseline uses BERT embeddings, not TF-IDF; the MobileBERT multilingual remark is untested.
Relevance to Our Project: INDIRECT. Cautionary example of spam/smishing label conflation, and a model for concept-level error analysis. Not target-language.
Research Gap or Opportunity: No non-English data; spam vs smishing distinction not tested.

Paper Title: PhishNet: A Real-Time, Scalable Ensemble Framework for Smishing Attack Detection Using Transformers and LLMs
Authors: Abeer Alhuzali; Qamar Al-Qahtani; Asmaa Niyazi; Lama Alshehri; Fatemah Alharbi
Journal/Conference: Computers, Materials & Continua, vol. 86, no. 1, pp. 1-19 (issue published 10 Nov 2025)
Research Objective: Classify messages as ham, spam or smishing in real time by combining RoBERTa with three LLMs through voting, using T5 augmentation for minority classes, and deploy it in a mobile app.
Dataset Used: Dataset1: Mishra and Soni SMS Phishing dataset. Dataset2: custom set with 997 smishing (SmishTank), 1,000 ham (UCI SMS Spam) and 1,000 synthetic 'spam' generated with the Faker library.
Dataset Size: Dataset1: 5,971 messages (paper text: 4,844 ham, 638 spam, 489 smishing); test set 2,371 (973 ham, 717 spam, 681 smishing). Dataset2: 2,997 messages; test set 600. 80/20 split.
Languages and Scripts: English only (the authors restrict to English because BERT-family models are English-pretrained).
Methodology and Models: Fine-tuned BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT (with and without preprocessing); GPT-OSS 120B, LLaMA3.3 70B, Qwen3 32B with zero-shot and few-shot prompts; confidence-weighted voting among LLMs, then majority vote with RoBERTa; T5 augmentation; FlutterFlow/Firebase app; usability test with 10 participants.
Key Findings: [Reported] RoBERTa accuracy 92% (Dataset1) and 100% (Dataset2) on hold-out; 5-fold CV on Dataset1 gave mean accuracy 0.729-0.753 with no significant differences (Friedman); ensemble 98% and 99% accuracy; abstract states average gain from 96% to 98.5%. All models struggled to separate spam from smishing. Mean SUS score 84.
Evaluation Metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, 95% CI, Friedman test, inference time, SUS.
Advantages: Three-class taxonomy; statistical testing; shows preprocessing gave no gain for transformers; working app.
Limitations: [Authors] Few datasets, English only, no adversarial evaluation, LLM compute cost (about 1.21 s per classification). [Our reading] The spam/smishing counts are stated in swapped order relative to another source and to the paper's own augmentation sentence; the Dataset1 test set holds 717 spam and 681 smishing messages, more than the 638 or 489 originals, which implies synthetic messages are in the test set; Dataset2 spam is synthetic and its classes come from different sources, which can make classes separable by source (RoBERTa 100%).
Relevance to Our Project: INDIRECT. Useful for a three-class taxonomy and as a warning on synthetic data; English only.
Research Gap or Opportunity: No non-English data; validity of T5/Faker-generated data against natural distributions untested.
Verification Status: VERIFIED (DATA REPOSITORY; FULL TEXT NOT RECHECKED)

Authors: Adnane Filali; Mohammad Shorfuzzaman; El Arbi Abdellaoui Alaoui; Mostafa Merras; Mohammed Es-Sabry; Achraf Berrajaa; Roobaea Alroobaea; Amr Yousef
Journal/Conference: Scientific Reports, vol. 16, Art. no. 7128 (published 3 Feb 2026)
Research Objective: Improve SMS spam classification under class imbalance with GAN-generated synthetic embeddings, evaluated over 5 embeddings x 8 models x 4 augmentation settings (120 configurations) on English and multilingual data.
Dataset Used: UCI SMS Spam Collection; 'Multilingual Spam Data' (Kaggle, rajnathpatel), which the authors state is machine-translated French, German and Hindi versions of the English corpus with an unspecified translation method.
Dataset Size: UCI: 5,572 messages (13.35% spam); stratified 80/20 split. Multilingual set size not separately stated in the text read.
Languages and Scripts: English; French, German, Hindi (machine-translated). No Malayalam.
Methodology and Models: SVM, LR, KNN, DT, SGD, RF, LSTM, BiLSTM; BoW, TF-IDF, Word2Vec, GloVe, BERT embeddings; augmentation by GAN (WGAN-GP on embeddings), SMOTE, ADASYN or none; five seeds for top configurations.
Key Findings: [Reported] Best: BERT + BiLSTM + GAN, F1 97.61% and accuracy 99.37% (monolingual), F1 94.44% (multilingual). Relevance to Our Project: INDIRECT. Template for factorial evaluation and FPR reporting. Translated data cannot stand in for naturally typed Manglish.
